{{Short description|Algebraic structure in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''quadratic algebra''' is an [[algebra over a ring]] for which the algebra extends the ring by a new element that satisfies a [[monic polynomial|monic]], [[quadratic polynomial]] with coefficients in the ring.

There are free and graded quadratic algebras.
==Free quadratic algebras==
Given a commutative [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'', and the ring of [[polynomial]]s ''R''[X], a free quadratic algebra may be defined as [[quotient ring]] by a polynomial [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]]:
"An ''R''-algebra of the form ''R''[X]/(X<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''a'' X &minus; ''b'') where X<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''a'' X &minus; ''b'' is a monic quadratic polynomial in ''R''[X] and (X<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''a'' X &minus; ''b'')
Is the ideal it generates, is a '''free quadratic algebra''' over R."<ref name = Hahn>Alexander J. Hahn (1994) ''Quadratic algebras, Clifford algebras, and Arithmetic Witt Groups'', page 5, Universitext, Springer, {{isbn|0-387-94110-X}}</ref>

Alternatively, a free quadratic extension of ''R'' is ''S'' = ''R'' ⊕ ''Rx'' with ''xx'' = ''ax'' + ''b'' for some ''a'' and ''b'' in R.<ref name=KK> K.  Kitamura (1973) "Quadratic extensions of a commutative ring", ''Osaka Journal of Mathematics'' 10: 15 to 20, available via [[Project Euclid]]</ref> Denote it ''S'' = (''R, a, b'').

Then (''R, a, b'') ≅ (''R, c, d'') [[iff]] there is a [[unit (ring theory)|unit]] &alpha; and an element &beta; of ''R'' such that<ref name=KK/> 
: ''c'' = &alpha;(''a'' &minus; 2 &beta; ) and
: ''d'' = &alpha;<sup>2</sup>(&beta; ''a'' + ''b'' &minus;&beta;<sup>2</sup>).

If ''R'' is taken as the ring Z of [[integer]]s, then the quadratic algebra <math>\Z[X]/(X^2 + 1)</math> is called the [[Gaussian integer]]s. 

If ''R'' is taken as the field of [[real number]]s, then there are three [[isomorphism class]]es of <math>\R[X]/(X^2 - a X - b)</math>:<ref name = Hahn/>{{rp|8}}
* if ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 4 ''b'' = 0, the [[dual number]]s
* if ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 4 ''b'' > 0, the [[split-complex number]]s
* if ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 4 ''b'' < 0, the [[complex number]]s.

Suppose the quadratic algebra ''S'' has basis {1,''z''} and <math>z^2 = a z + b. </math> Then an [[involution (mathematics)|involution]] &sigma; on S is given by <math>\sigma(z) = a - z, </math> and if <math>x = \lambda + \mu z, </math> then <math>\sigma(x) = \lambda + \mu a - \mu z.</math>

Trace and norm are then defined using the involution:<ref>{{cite book | last=Knus | first=Max-Albert | authorlink=Max-Albert Knus | title=Quadratic and Hermitian forms over Rings | series=Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften | volume=294 | location=Berlin etc. | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=1991 | isbn=3-540-52117-8 | zbl=0756.11008 | page=4 }}</ref>
:<math>tr(x) = x + \sigma(x) = 2 \lambda + \mu a \in R ,</math>
:<math>n(x) = x \sigma(x) = \lambda^2 - \lambda \mu a - \mu^2 b \in R.</math>

== Graded quadratic algebras ==

A '''graded quadratic algebra''' ''A'' is determined by a [[vector space]] of generators ''V'' = ''A''<sub>1</sub> and a subspace of homogeneous quadratic relations ''S'' ⊂ ''V'' ⊗ ''V''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Polishchuk |first1=Alexander |last2=Positselski |first2=Leonid |year=2005 |title=Quadratic algebras |volume=37 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5_ZrCKU4NpAC&pg=PA6 |page=6 |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |location=Providence, R.I. |series=University Lecture Series |isbn=978-0-8218-3834-1 |mr=2177131}}</ref> Thus

: <math> A=T(V)/\langle S\rangle </math>

and inherits its grading from the [[tensor algebra]] ''T''(''V''). 

If the subspace of relations is instead allowed to  also contain inhomogeneous degree 2 elements,  i.e. ''S'' ⊂ ''k'' ⊕ ''V'' ⊕ (''V'' ⊗ ''V''), this construction results in a '''filtered quadratic algebra'''.

A graded quadratic algebra ''A'' as above admits a '''quadratic dual''': the quadratic algebra generated by ''V''<sup>*</sup> and with quadratic relations forming the orthogonal complement of ''S'' in ''V''<sup>*</sup> ⊗ ''V''<sup>*</sup>.

A  quadratic algebra may be a [[filtered algebra]] generated by degree one elements, with defining relations of degree 2. It was pointed out by [[Yuri Manin]] that such algebras play an important role in the theory of [[quantum group]]s. The most important class of graded quadratic algebras is [[Koszul algebra]]s.

A '''quadratic-linear algebra''' is an [[algebra over a field]] with a [[Presentation of a group|presentation]] such that all relations are sums of monomials of degrees 1 or 2 in the generators. They were introduced by {{harvs|txt|last1=Polishchuk|last2=Positselski|year=2005|loc=p.101}}. An example is the [[universal enveloping algebra]] of a [[Lie algebra]], with generators a basis of the Lie algebra and relations of the form&nbsp;''XY''&nbsp;–&nbsp;''YX''&nbsp;–&nbsp;[''X'',&nbsp;''Y'']&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.

== Examples ==

* The [[tensor algebra]], [[symmetric algebra]] and [[exterior algebra]] of a finite-dimensional [[vector space]] are graded quadratic (in fact, Koszul) algebras.
* The [[universal enveloping algebra]] of a finite-dimensional [[Lie algebra]] is a filtered quadratic algebra.
* The [[Clifford algebra]] of a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a [[quadratic form]] is a filtered quadratic algebra.
* The [[Weyl algebra]] of a finite-dimensional [[symplectic vector space]] is a filtered quadratic algebra.
